title: Stones Into Schools: Promoting Peace With Books, Not Bombs, in Afghanistan and Pakistan
author: Greg Mortenson
target_audience: Supporters of educational initiatives in conflict zones
Educators and students of global studies
General audiences interested in Afghanistan, Pakistan, or humanitarian work
core_themes: Education as a foundation for peace
Challenges of aid work in conflict regions
primary_purpose: To chronicle Greg Mortenson’s continued efforts to promote education, especially for girls, in remote and volatile regions of Afghanistan and Pakistan, and to illustrate how community-based education can foster peace in areas afflicted by violence.

structure_format.organization: Linear chronicle following the work of the Central Asia Institute after events described in the previous book, with digressions into personal stories, profiles of helpers, and local history
features: Profiles of local allies and leaders
Exploration of logistical, cultural, and ethical challenges in aid work

key_concepts_lessons: Sustainable change is rooted in partnership with local communities.
Educating girls is a powerful tool for societal transformation and peace-building.
Aid must be tailored to cultural contexts and cannot be imposed top-down.
Trust, patience, and humility are essential for effective humanitarian work.
Small dedicated groups can make significant impacts despite major obstacles.
Listening to local voices and operating with cultural sensitivity prevents many common failures of foreign aid.
notable_features: Real stories from Afghanistan and Pakistan’s most dangerous regions
Focus on collaboration with tribal elders, especially in Afghanistan’s Wakhan Corridor
Highlights the role of education in fighting extremism and promoting stability
Continuations from Mortenson’s earlier work in 'Three Cups of Tea'
Acknowledges missteps and challenges in charity work
cultural_historical_context: Published in a time of Western military intervention in Afghanistan and Pakistan, the book contrasts military approaches with education-based humanitarianism, and reflects growing global awareness of the power of educating girls and grassroots development.
reception_impact: A national bestseller and widely discussed in humanitarian and educational circles
Praised for its inspirational stories and advocacy for girls’ education
Later scrutiny and controversy regarding Mortenson's financial and factual mismanagement somewhat affected legacy
Continued to raise awareness about grassroots development needs in conflict regions
comparable_titles: Three Cups of Tea by Greg Mortenson and David Oliver Relin
I Am Malala by Malala Yousafzai
The Bookseller of Kabul by Åsne Seierstad
Half the Sky by Nicholas D. Kristof and Sheryl WuDunn
